notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • The concepts and the resolution algorithm — RFC 1034: Domain Names — Concepts and Facilities

  • Wire format, size limits, port 53 — RFC 1035: Domain Names — Implementation and Specification

  • Why 512 bytes stopped being the ceiling — RFC 6891: Extension Mechanisms for DNS (EDNS(0))

  • TCP is required, not a fallback curiosity — RFC 7766: DNS Transport over TCP

  • The four-server walk, drawn clearly — Cloudflare: What is DNS?

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
Who does the walking — client or resolver? The recursive resolver. The stub client asks once and waits.
The four parties in a cold lookup? Stub → recursive resolver → root → TLD → authoritative.
What do root and TLD servers return? Referrals (NS records), never the final answer.
Classic UDP message ceiling, and what raised it? 512 octets; EDNS(0) advertises a larger payload.
Is TCP optional? No — RFC 7766 makes both UDP and TCP required.

🪞 How to use this section: First pass — answer cold, mark misses. Read the note. Second pass — re-test only the misses. Third pass (day before) — full re-test.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

Your application asks a stub resolver, which asks a recursive resolver, and that resolver does all the work: it queries a root server, which refers it to the .com TLD servers, which refer it to the zone's authoritative servers, which return the answer. The client sees one question and one answer; the four-step walk happens on the resolver's side and is almost entirely served from its cache in practice. The detail that matters operationally is that root and TLD servers never return your record — they return referrals, so every layer in that chain is a delegation you depend on.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification

Walk the resolution of api.example.com on a completely cold cache.

The stub resolver in the OS sends one recursive query to whatever resolver /etc/resolv.conf names, and then waits — it does no walking itself. The recursive resolver starts at a root server, which is authoritative for nothing useful but knows the delegation for com, so it returns NS records for the .com TLD servers plus glue records giving their addresses. The resolver then asks a .com server, which returns the NS records for example.com's authoritative nameservers, again with glue.

The third query goes to one of those authoritative servers, which finally returns the A record for api.example.com with the authoritative-answer bit set. Three referrals, one answer, and every step cached at its own TTL — so the next lookup for anything under .com skips the root, and the next lookup under example.com skips both root and TLD. That is why a cold resolution can take a few hundred milliseconds and a warm one is effectively free, and why measuring DNS latency in aggregate tells you almost nothing.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

Which resolver should your infrastructure use — the cloud provider's, a public one, or your own?

🎯 Really testing: whether you treat the resolver as a dependency with a failure mode, or as ambient infrastructure that always works.

The provider's resolver is the default and usually right inside a VPC, because it also serves private zones, instance metadata naming and endpoint records that a public resolver cannot see. On AWS that is Route 53 Resolver, reachable at the VPC base address plus two or at the link-local 169.254.169.253. The catch is a hard quota: the link-local path is limited to 1,024 packets per second per network interface, and that limit is shared with the metadata service and NTP. A chatty container host doing per-request lookups hits it, and the failure is dropped queries, not a clean error.

A public resolver like 1.1.1.1 or 8.8.8.8 buys you anycast reach and good uptime, but it cannot resolve your private zones and it puts your resolution path outside your control — Cloudflare's own 1.1.1.1 outage in July 2025 took the service down globally for 62 minutes after a configuration change withdrew its route announcements. Running your own resolver is worth it at scale, where a node-local cache in front of the cluster resolver absorbs the repeated lookups that would otherwise hit the quota. My default is the provider's resolver plus a node-local cache, with a public resolver configured only as an explicit secondary for external names.

Tier 3 — Edge case / scaling

What runs out first when a service does DNS lookups on every request?

📍 Seen in the wild: the standard failure of a containerised fleet that disabled or never had client-side caching.

Query rate runs out first, and in a cloud environment there is a documented ceiling rather than a soft degradation: 1,024 packets per second per network interface to the link-local resolver on AWS, shared with the metadata and time services and explicitly not increasable. A container host presents as one interface, so all its pods spend one budget. Client-side UDP socket buffers are the second limit, and dropped responses look identical to a slow resolver.

It presents as intermittent tail latency with no error signature. Dropped queries are retried after the stub resolver's timeout — typically seconds — so p99 develops a shelf at the retry interval while p50 stays flat, and nothing logs a failure because the retry succeeds. The diagnosis is that latency correlates with fresh connections rather than with the downstream service; the fix is caching, either a node-local DNS cache or connection pooling so the lookup happens once per pool. (→ 32-ttl-and-caching-layers.md)

Tier 4 — Open-ended design (architect-level)

Design the DNS path for a multi-region service whose clients are both browsers and internal workloads.

🎯 Really testing: whether you separate the public and private resolution paths and give each its own failure story, rather than drawing one box marked "DNS".

The highest-stakes constraint is that DNS is the first dependency in every request and has no fallback: if resolution fails, nothing else in the design matters. So make the authoritative side survive the loss of any one provider — nameservers at two independent DNS providers carrying the same zone, with enough NS records published that losing one is a resolver retry rather than an outage. A single authoritative provider is the classic single point of failure.

The public path then uses the authoritative service's own routing to send browsers to a nearby region — latency or geolocation routing with health checks attached — while accepting that client caching makes DNS a slow failover mechanism. The private path is separate: a private zone resolved only inside the network by the provider's resolver, with a node-local cache in front so per-request lookups never reach the quota. Internal names never appear in the public zone.

The failure I would monitor first is not resolution errors but stale answers — the gap between publishing a change and clients acting on it. That gap is your record TTL plus the negative-cache TTL if anything ever returned NXDOMAIN plus whatever the runtime holds, and it decides whether a DNS failover is a two-minute or a two-hour event.

4. Quick Comparison Table

Server Answers with Caches? Who runs it What breaks if it fails
Stub resolver (OS) The resolver's answer Sometimes, briefly Your OS / libc The single host
Recursive resolver The final answer Yes, per TTL — the important cache Cloud provider, ISP, or you Every client pointed at it
Root server A referral to the TLD No The 13 root operators (anycast) Nothing, immediately — heavily cached
TLD server A referral to the zone No The registry (Verisign for .com) New resolutions under that TLD
Authoritative server The record itself No Your DNS provider Your domain, once caches expire

6. Mechanism & Math (How It Actually Works)

The mechanism has one structural idea — delegation — and everything else follows from it. No server holds the whole namespace; each one holds a zone and points downward with NS records, plus glue address records when the nameserver's own name lives inside the zone being delegated. That is why root and TLD servers are never a latency problem in steady state: their referrals have long TTLs and are cached almost permanently, so the only query that actually leaves your resolver most of the time is the last one.

The size limits are the other half of the mechanism, and they explain the fallbacks. RFC 1035 caps a label at 63 octets, a full name at 255, and a UDP message at 512, all on port 53. Anything larger than 512 sets the truncation bit and the resolver retries over TCP — which RFC 7766 makes a required part of every implementation, not an optional extra. EDNS(0) avoids most of that by letting the requester advertise a larger UDP payload; RFC 6891 discusses 4096 as a starting point with a 1280–1410 fallback that fits inside one Ethernet frame. This matters in practice because a firewall that blocks DNS over TCP, or drops fragmented UDP, produces a failure where small answers resolve and large ones — a zone with many records, or DNSSEC — hang.

The arithmetic worth carrying is the cold-versus-warm split. A cold resolution is three sequential round trips plus the answer, so on a path with 30 ms round trips it costs roughly 120 ms; a warm one is a cache read at effectively zero. Since referrals are cached far longer than records, the steady-state cost of a lookup is one round trip to the authoritative server, and the cost you actually feel is the client-side cache miss rate rather than anything about the hierarchy.

7. Why It Matters in Production

The observable is time-to-first-byte on cold connections, and DNS is the first term in it — before TCP, before TLS, before your server sees anything. It is also the term with the widest distribution, because a cache hit costs nothing and a miss costs multiple round trips, so DNS shows up in p99 long before it shows up in p50. Any latency budget that starts at "the request arrives" has already omitted it.

It matters more as a dependency than as a latency term, though. Every request in the system begins with a name lookup, and there is no degraded mode — a failed lookup is a failed request, retried at the stub resolver's timeout rather than yours. That is why DNS incidents present as total rather than partial outages, and why the resolution path deserves the same redundancy thinking as a database.

8. Command / Config / Code Example

# Watch the actual delegation walk — root, then TLD, then authoritative.
dig +trace api.example.com

# What a single resolver returns, with timing and which server answered.
dig @1.1.1.1 api.example.com +noall +answer +stats

# Is the answer authoritative or cached? Look for the aa flag and the TTL counting down.
dig @ns1.example.com api.example.com   # aa flag set, TTL at its configured value
dig @1.1.1.1 api.example.com           # no aa flag, TTL already decremented

# Does the path survive a large answer? Forces TCP; fails where DNS/TCP is blocked.
dig +tcp DNSKEY example.com

+trace is the one to know cold: it makes the resolver's iterative walk visible, which is the difference between reasoning about the hierarchy and having watched it.

9. Concrete Trace (Step-by-Step with Real Data)

dig +trace api.example.com from a cold cache, on a path with ~30 ms round trips.

📥 [0] stub → resolver: A api.example.com, RD=1              t = 0 ms
    │
    ▼
🌐 [1] resolver → root (anycast, ~10 ms away)
        ← referral: NS a.gtld-servers.net … + glue A records
        TTL 172800 — cached for two days                      t ≈ 10 ms
    │
    ▼
🗂️ [2] resolver → com TLD
        ← referral: NS ns1.example.com, ns2.example.com + glue
        TTL 172800                                            t ≈ 45 ms
    │
    ▼
📇 [3] resolver → ns1.example.com
        ← api.example.com. 300 IN A 203.0.113.7, flags: qr aa
        TTL 300 — this is the short one                       t ≈ 90 ms
    │
    ▼
✅ [4] resolver → stub: answer cached 300 s                   t ≈ 95 ms
        second lookup, 1 s later: answer in 0.4 ms, TTL 299

  1. The stub does one query and the resolver does three. RD=1 (recursion desired) is the whole contract — the client asks someone else to do the work, which is why client-side DNS tuning is about caching rather than about the hierarchy.

  2. Root and TLD referrals carry two-day TTLs, so steps 1 and 2 essentially never repeat. In steady state the resolver goes straight to the authoritative server, which is why hierarchy depth is not a latency concern and why "DNS is slow" nearly always means a short record TTL and a poor cache hit rate.

  3. The aa flag distinguishes an origin answer from a cached one, and the decrementing TTL is the second tell: an answer with TTL 299 against a configured 300 has been cached for one second. Reading that number is how you judge staleness.

  4. The 300-second record TTL is the only number here you control, and it decides how long a change takes to take effect. Everything else is set by the root and TLD operators.

10. When TO Use This

When you are diagnosing a slow or failed connection and have not yet ruled out the name lookup. It is the first thing in the path and the one people skip, and dig +trace settles it in seconds.

When designing anything whose availability matters, because the delegation chain is a dependency list: registrar, registry, your DNS provider, your resolver. Each is a party that can take you down without touching your infrastructure.

When a change is not taking effect. The resolution path plus the caching layers is the entire explanation, and knowing which server is authoritative lets you compare the origin answer against what clients are actually seeing.

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

Do not reason about DNS latency from the cold path. The three-referral walk is what people draw, and it is almost never what happens: referrals are cached for days, so the real cost is one round trip or zero. Optimising the hierarchy is optimising something that already does not run.

Do not put a public resolver in front of private names. It cannot see your private zones, and configuring it as a fallback produces a system that resolves internal names most of the time and NXDOMAIN occasionally — which then gets cached. Split-horizon resolution needs the provider's resolver or your own. (→ 34-private-dns-service-discovery.md)

Do not assume UDP is enough. Blocking DNS over TCP, or dropping fragmented UDP responses, gives you a network where small answers work and large ones hang — a failure that looks like an application bug and survives a long time because the common case is fine.

Do not treat the resolver as infinite. Cloud resolvers have documented quotas — 1,024 packets per second per interface on AWS, shared with the metadata and time services — and exceeding them drops queries silently rather than returning an error.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "The client walks the hierarchy from root downward."

✅ Reality: The stub resolver sends one recursive query and waits. The walk belongs to the recursive resolver, which is also where the cache that matters lives. Getting this backwards leads to client-side fixes for a server-side property.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): "Root servers are a bottleneck, and there are only 13 of them."

✅ Reality: There are 13 root server identities, each anycast to hundreds of physical locations, and their referrals carry TTLs measured in days. In steady state your resolver contacts a root server almost never. The number 13 is a limit on how many addresses fit in a 512-byte response, not a count of machines.

❌ Misconception: "A DNS answer is either right or missing."

✅ Reality: It can be stale, and staleness is the normal state — every answer you receive from a resolver has already been cached for some part of its TTL. The interesting question is never "is DNS working" but "how old is this answer and who else is holding one".

13. Tech Discussion Traps

Describing the cold path as if it were the normal one. Reciting root → TLD → authoritative is correct and incomplete; the follow-up is what actually happens on the millionth request, and the answer is a cache hit. Say both.

Confusing the recursive resolver with the authoritative server. They have opposite jobs — one caches and never owns data, the other owns data and never caches. Nearly every DNS design question turns on which side of that line a problem sits, so blurring it makes the rest of the answer unreliable.

Skipping the transport. UDP with a 512-byte limit, EDNS(0) to raise it, TCP as a required fallback — that is where the "works for most domains, hangs for one" failures come from, and it is the detail that shows you have debugged DNS rather than read about it.

Treating DNS as infrastructure rather than as a dependency. It has providers, quotas, delegations and single points of failure like anything else. An answer that never names who could take your domain down is a description, not a design.

14. Key Numbers & Benchmarks

Metric Value Context Source
DNS port 53, TCP and UDP Both required, not UDP-preferred RFC 1035 §4.2 · RFC 7766 §5
Label / name limits 63 / 255 octets Why very deep names fail oddly RFC 1035 §2.3.4
Classic UDP message limit 512 octets Larger sets TC bit → retry over TCP RFC 1035 §4.2.1
EDNS(0) payload 4096 as a starting point; 1280–1410 fallback The fallback fits one Ethernet frame RFC 6891 §6.2.5
Maximum TTL 2,147,483,647 s (2³¹−1) Signed-bit quirk: top bit set should read as 0 RFC 2181 §8
Root server identities 13 addresses, each anycast A response-size limit, not a machine count RFC 1035 §4.2.1 (512-byte cap)
AWS resolver query quota 1,024 pps per network interface Shared with IMDS and NTP; not increasable AWS VPC DNS docs
AWS resolver addresses VPC base + 2, or 169.254.169.253 The link-local one carries the quota AWS VPC DNS docs

15. Trade-offs & Performance Considerations

Dimension Trade-off
⏱️ Latency Cold lookup is three sequential round trips; warm is free. DNS lives in p99, not p50, which is why aggregate DNS latency is a useless metric
💰 Cost Negligible per query, but query volume is a real constraint against a quota — and a node-local cache is cheaper than raising anything
🔒 Security / visibility Plaintext by default: resolvers see every name you look up, and answers are forgeable without DNSSEC. Encrypted transports move the trust rather than removing it
📈 Scale Bounded by resolver query rate, not by zone size. The ceiling is per network interface in cloud environments, so container density is the multiplier
🔧 Ops complexity The delegation chain adds three parties you do not run — registrar, registry, DNS provider — each able to take the domain down
🐛 Debuggability Unusually good: dig +trace shows the whole walk, and the aa flag plus a decrementing TTL tells you whether an answer is fresh and how old it is

16. Real World Usage

The 2021 Facebook outage is the canonical example of the delegation chain failing from above. A configuration change withdrew the BGP routes to Facebook's own nameserver prefixes, so resolvers worldwide could not reach the authoritative servers and returned SERVFAIL — records fine, servers fine, path to them gone. It is the clearest demonstration that DNS availability is not a property of your zone data. Cloudflare's 1.1.1.1 incident in July 2025 is the same failure on the resolver side: a configuration error linked the resolver's prefixes to a pre-production service, its routes were withdrawn globally, and it was unavailable for 62 minutes. If your infrastructure resolves through a single public resolver, that is your outage too.

The Kubernetes version is quota rather than reachability. A dense node whose pods resolve per request shares one interface's query budget — on AWS a documented 1,024 packets per second, shared with metadata and time. The standard remedy, a node-local DNS cache, is a caching fix for what presents as a networking problem.

17. Acronym Decoder

"DNS — Domain Name System" is universally known and its expansion teaches nothing about the mechanism, so it is skipped per the template rule. The acronyms in this section that do carry mechanism (SOA, NS, TTL, SRV, NXDOMAIN) are decoded where they are used, in 31-record-types.md and 32-ttl-and-caching-layers.md.

  • Record types you'll use (31-record-types.md) — what the authoritative server actually returns.

  • DNS as an outage cause (35-dns-as-an-outage-cause.md) — the failure catalogue built on this path.

🔀 Alternatives / Competing approaches

  • Service discovery via a registry (Consul, etcd, a control plane) — replaces DNS for internal names with something that has push semantics instead of TTL semantics.

  • Hard-coded addresses or a service mesh's own resolution — removes DNS from the hot path entirely, at the cost of a separate configuration distribution problem.

19. System Design Application

Skipped — this note describes a resolution mechanism rather than a component whose placement is the design question. The architect-level treatment (multi-provider authoritative DNS, split public and private paths, resolver quotas) is discharged by the Section 3 Tier 4 follow-up, and the system-level caching and failover story belongs to 32-ttl-and-caching-layers.md and 33-dns-load-balancing.md.

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • The CNAME exclusivity rule — RFC 2181 §10.1: Clarifications to the DNS Specification

  • SRV format, priority and weight — RFC 2782: A DNS RR for specifying the location of services

  • What each type is for, quickly — Cloudflare: DNS records

  • ALIAS is a vendor extension, not a standard — Amazon Route 53: Choosing between alias and non-alias records

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
Why can't a zone apex have a CNAME? A name with a CNAME may have no other records — and the apex needs SOA and NS.
What is ALIAS / ANAME? A provider-side extension that resolves the target and answers with A/AAAA.
Which record carries the negative-cache TTL? SOA, in its MINIMUM field.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

Six types cover almost everything you touch. A and AAAA map a name to an IPv4 or IPv6 address; CNAME aliases one name to another and, crucially, forbids any other record at that name; NS delegates a subtree to other nameservers; MX routes mail with a preference value; TXT holds arbitrary strings and in practice holds SPF, DKIM and domain-verification tokens; SRV names a host and port for a service, which is what makes it useful for discovery. The gap everyone hits is that the apex cannot be a CNAME, which is why providers invented ALIAS.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification

Why can't example.com be a CNAME to your load balancer, and what do you use instead?

Because RFC 2181 makes the types mutually exclusive at a name: either exactly one CNAME exists there, or one or more non-CNAME records do — never both. A zone apex is obliged to carry an SOA record and its NS records, so it already holds non-CNAME data, and adding a CNAME would violate the rule. Resolvers that encounter both behave inconsistently, which is why providers reject the configuration outright rather than letting you discover it later.

The workaround is a provider-side extension, marketed as ALIAS, ANAME or "CNAME flattening" depending on the vendor. Route 53's alias record is the reference implementation: you point the apex at an AWS resource, and Route 53 resolves the target itself and answers the query with A or AAAA records, so what appears on the wire is a perfectly ordinary address record. That is also why dig shows type A rather than CNAME. The trade-offs are that it is not portable between providers, and its TTL is not yours to set — Route 53 uses the target's — so an apex record gives up the TTL control you might want during a migration.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

When would you reach for SRV rather than a plain A record plus a known port?

🎯 Really testing: whether you know SRV exists and also why almost nothing on the web uses it.

SRV is the right shape whenever the port is not fixed by convention and the client is willing to look it up: _service._proto.name returns priority, weight, port and target, so one lookup gives both where to connect and on which port, with priority selecting a tier and weight distributing within it. That is genuinely useful for internal service discovery, for SIP and XMPP, and for Kubernetes headless services, where each backing pod gets an SRV record naming its port.

It has essentially no reach on the web because browsers do not consult SRV records — HTTP clients assume 80 and 443, so publishing SRV for a website achieves nothing. The other limitation is that the weight field was designed for static capacity differences rather than live load; RFC 2782 is explicit that larger weights get a proportionately higher selection probability, which is round-robin with fixed ratios, not load balancing. So SRV is a discovery mechanism for clients you control, and it is not a substitute for a load balancer. (→ 34-private-dns-service-discovery.md)

4. Quick Comparison Table

Type Holds Standard? When you'd actually use it
A / AAAA An IPv4 / IPv6 address RFC 1035 · RFC 3596 The terminal answer; everything else eventually resolves to these
CNAME Another name RFC 1035 Subdomain pointing at a vendor hostname — never at an apex
ALIAS / ANAME Another name, resolved by the provider ❌ Vendor extension Apex pointing at a load balancer or CDN; the CNAME workaround
NS Nameservers for a subtree RFC 1034 Delegation — the mechanism the whole hierarchy runs on
MX Mail host + preference RFC 1035 Mail routing; lower preference is tried first
TXT Arbitrary strings RFC 1035 SPF, DKIM, DMARC, and every "verify you own this domain" flow
SRV Priority, weight, port, target RFC 2782 Internal discovery where the port is not conventional
SOA Zone parameters incl. MINIMUM RFC 1035 · RFC 2308 One per zone; its MINIMUM sets the negative-cache TTL
PTR A name, for reverse lookup RFC 1035 Reverse DNS — mail reputation, and log readability
CAA Which CAs may issue RFC 8659 Constraining certificate issuance for your domain

6. Mechanism & Math (How It Actually Works)

The loop at the top is the mechanism worth internalising: a CNAME does not return an address, it returns a new question, and the resolver restarts. Chains therefore cost extra round trips on a cold cache and are a real latency term when a CNAME points at a CNAME pointing at a CDN hostname. It is also why the exclusivity rule exists — if a name could hold both a CNAME and an A record, a resolver would have two contradictory instructions.

The two failure outcomes on the right are distinct and worth naming separately. NXDOMAIN means the name does not exist at all; NODATA means the name exists but has no record of the type asked for — a name with only an MX record queried for AAAA returns NODATA, not NXDOMAIN. Both are cached using the zone's SOA MINIMUM rather than any record's TTL, which is the connection to the caching note and the reason a missing AAAA can be sticky. (→ 32-ttl-and-caching-layers.md)

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

Do not chain CNAMEs. Each hop is another resolution the client waits for on a cold cache, and long chains hit provider limits and confuse debugging. One hop to a vendor hostname is normal; three is a latency bug someone will eventually have to unpick.

Do not put an ALIAS-style record in a design that must be portable. It is a provider feature with no standard behind it, so a multi-provider or provider-migration plan has to solve the apex problem again at the other end — and the TTL is not yours to control.

Do not use TXT as a general-purpose key-value store. It works, which is the problem: large TXT sets push responses past the UDP limit and into TCP, and a firewall that blocks DNS over TCP turns that into an intermittent resolution failure for one domain. (→ 30-dns-resolution.md)

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "NXDOMAIN means the record I asked for is missing."

✅ Reality: It means the name does not exist. A name that exists with other record types returns NODATA — an empty answer with a successful status. The distinction matters because clients and libraries treat them differently, and because both are negative-cached from the SOA rather than from anything you set on the record.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): "ALIAS is just a nicer CNAME."

✅ Reality: It is not a DNS record type at all. The provider resolves the target on its side and answers with plain A or AAAA records, which is why it works at the apex and why the wire format shows no trace of it. That also means it is non-portable and its TTL follows the target rather than your configuration.

18. Connections (Typed Knowledge Graph)

📚 Reference Links

  • TTL semantics and the maximum value — RFC 2181 §8: Clarifications to the DNS Specification

  • Negative caching — the layer people forget — RFC 2308: Negative Caching of DNS Queries (DNS NCACHE)

  • Caching in the original model — RFC 1034 §4.3.4: Domain Names — Concepts and Facilities

  • Alias records and the TTL you do not control — Amazon Route 53: Choosing between alias and non-alias records

  • Where the query budget runs out — Amazon VPC: Amazon DNS concepts

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
How is the negative-cache TTL derived? min(SOA MINIMUM, TTL of the SOA record) — not from the missing record.
Maximum legal TTL? 2,147,483,647 s (2³¹−1); top bit set should be read as 0.
Which cache does lowering a TTL not affect? Any answer already cached — the old TTL runs out first.
The JVM's historic trap? It could cache DNS answers for the process lifetime, ignoring TTL.
Why did your change "not take"? Some layer holds an answer issued before you made it.

🪞 How to use this section: First pass — answer cold, mark misses. Read the note. Second pass — re-test only the misses. Third pass (day before) — full re-test.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

A TTL is the number of seconds any cache may hold an answer, and the answer is cached independently at every layer — recursive resolver, OS stub, application runtime, and often the connection pool that resolved once and never looked again. Lowering a TTL only affects answers handed out after the change, so a record that was published at an hour has an hour of stale copies in the world no matter what you do next. That is the whole explanation for "my DNS change didn't take", and it is also why DNS is a slow failover mechanism.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification

Enumerate the caches between your zone file and a running application.

Four, and they are independent. The recursive resolver holds the authoritative answer for its TTL and is the one that matters most, because it serves many clients — its copy decrements visibly, so a dig against it showing TTL 42 means the answer has 42 seconds left. The OS stub resolver may cache too: systemd-resolved and Windows both do, macOS does via mDNSResponder, and a plain glibc without nscd does not, which is why behaviour differs between a container and a laptop.

Then the two that surprise people. The language runtime caches: the JVM historically cached successful lookups for the lifetime of the process unless networkaddress.cache.ttl was set, and negative lookups for ten seconds — modern JDKs default to 30 seconds positive, but the setting is still the thing to check rather than assume. And the connection pool is the sneakiest, because it does not cache DNS at all; it caches the connection, which was opened to an address resolved once at pool creation. A pool with long-lived keepalives will keep talking to a decommissioned address for as long as the socket stays up, regardless of every TTL in the chain. (→ Connection pooling & keep-alive, Section 14)

Tier 2 — Trade-off

What TTL would you set, and what does the choice cost you?

🎯 Really testing: whether you can name the failover-time-versus-query-volume trade rather than reciting "300 is standard".

The TTL is a direct trade between how fast a change propagates and how many queries you serve. A 60-second TTL means a change is live within about a minute and the record is re-fetched roughly once a minute per resolver — which for a large audience is a real query rate against your authoritative provider and, if the resolvers sit inside your own network, against your resolver quota. A 24-hour TTL means one query per resolver per day and a full day of stale answers if you need to move.

So I set it by how urgently the record might need to change. Records pointing at a load balancer or a failover target get 60 seconds, because their whole purpose is to be changed under pressure. Records that essentially never move — the MX for a mail provider, a TXT verification, a CNAME to a CDN hostname that itself has a short TTL — get hours. And the operational discipline that matters more than the number is lowering the TTL before a planned migration, waiting out the old TTL, then migrating: doing it in the other order means the change is gated by the value you were trying to escape. The one caveat is that a very short TTL buys less than it looks like, because resolvers may floor it and the layers above still cache.

Tier 3 — Edge case / scaling

A record was accidentally deleted for two minutes. Why is the outage longer than two minutes?

📍 Seen in the wild: the mechanism behind a large share of "we fixed it but it's still broken" incidents.

Negative caching is why, and it runs on a completely different TTL from the one you were watching. When an authoritative server answers NXDOMAIN or NODATA, RFC 2308 says resolvers cache that negative answer for min(SOA MINIMUM, the SOA record's own TTL) — a value taken from the zone's SOA, not from the record that was missing. Zones commonly ship with an SOA minimum of an hour or more, so a two-minute deletion can produce an hour of cached NXDOMAIN across every resolver that happened to ask during the window. RFC 2308 notes that values of one to three hours have been found to work well and that anything over a day is problematic — which tells you both that hours are normal and that the failure is well known.

It presents as a partial, geographically random recovery. Resolvers that never asked during the window are fine; resolvers that did are stuck until their negative entry expires, so some users recover instantly and others in an hour, with no pattern the on-call engineer can act on. Nothing in your monitoring shows the negative cache, because it lives in infrastructure you do not run. The only real mitigations are preventive: keep the SOA minimum low enough that a mistake is recoverable, and treat record deletion as a change requiring the same care as a deploy.

Tier 4 — Open-ended design (architect-level)

Design a region failover that uses DNS, and be honest about how long it takes.

📍 Seen in the wild: the moment a "DNS failover" design meets an actual RTO requirement.

The highest-stakes constraint is that DNS failover time is not the TTL — it is the sum of every cache in the chain plus the detection delay before the record changes at all. Health checks take tens of seconds to declare a region down; the change then reaches only resolvers whose copy has expired, so the record TTL is the second term; OS and runtime caches add a third; and pools holding open sockets to the failed region add a fourth that no TTL bounds. A design promising a 60-second RTO because the TTL is 60 seconds is wrong by a factor set by client behaviour you do not control.

So: 60-second TTL on the failover records, health checks at the authoritative provider so the change is automatic rather than human-triggered, and an RTO stated in minutes with a long tail. Where the requirement is genuinely tight, DNS is the wrong layer — anycast moves traffic in routing-convergence time with no cache to wait out, and a global L7 load balancer with a stable address moves it per request. DNS failover is right for "recover in minutes without new infrastructure" and wrong for "recover in seconds".

The failure I would monitor first is residual traffic to the failed region after cutover. It measures every cache in the chain at once, turns a theoretical RTO into a measured one, and is the only way to find out which clients ignore TTLs before an incident tells you.

4. Quick Comparison Table

Cache layer Honours record TTL? Typical hold How to inspect Why it bites
Recursive resolver Yes — decrements visibly The record TTL dig @resolver name and read the TTL Serves many clients from one stale copy
OS stub / systemd-resolved Usually Seconds to the record TTL resolvectl statistics, resolvectl flush-caches Differs between container and host
Language runtime (JVM et al.) Historically no Process lifetime if misconfigured Check networkaddress.cache.ttl Survives every flush you can think of
Connection pool Not a DNS cache at all As long as the socket lives Pool metrics; connection age Unbounded by any TTL — the real long tail
Negative cache (NXDOMAIN) No — uses the SOA min(SOA MINIMUM, SOA TTL); hours is common dig the SOA; read MINIMUM A brief mistake becomes a long outage

6. Mechanism & Math (How It Actually Works)

The arithmetic is a sum of independent holds, and only the first term is the TTL you set. Propagation delay is detection + remaining record TTL + OS cache + runtime cache + connection lifetime. The remaining record TTL is uniformly distributed between zero and the full TTL across resolvers, so the mean wait is half the TTL and the worst case is the whole of it — which is why a 300-second TTL gives an average of 150 seconds and a tail at 300 for the resolver layer alone. Everything after that is additive and largely outside your control.

Negative caching runs on a separate clock. RFC 2308 derives the negative TTL from the zone's SOA — min(SOA MINIMUM, the SOA's own TTL) — so it is invisible in the record you were editing. This is the single most common reason a fix does not appear to work: the positive TTL was 60 seconds, the SOA minimum was 3600, and the resolvers that asked during the broken window are holding NXDOMAIN for an hour.

The TTL field itself has one quirk worth knowing. RFC 2181 defines it as an unsigned value from 0 to 2³¹−1 carried in a 32-bit field, and says implementations receiving a value with the top bit set should treat it as zero rather than as an enormous number. That is why a misconfigured TTL sometimes produces no caching instead of permanent caching — the failure is the opposite of the intuitive one.

Zero is legal and means "do not cache" — occasionally right for a record that must always be fresh, almost always wrong at scale, because every client then pays a full lookup per connection out of a fixed resolver quota.

7. Why It Matters in Production

The observable is change-propagation time, and it is the number that turns a migration plan into a schedule. Every cutover — a new load balancer, a region move, a provider change — is gated by it, and teams routinely discover the true value during the migration rather than before it, because the TTL they were watching was only the first of four terms.

It also matters as the ceiling on DNS-based failover. If the design says "we fail over via DNS", the recovery time objective is bounded below by this sum, and no amount of health-check tuning improves the cached-answer part. Knowing that early is the difference between choosing DNS failover deliberately and discovering its limits during an incident.

8. Command / Config / Code Example

# Read the remaining TTL from a resolver — repeat it and watch the number fall.
dig @1.1.1.1 api.example.com +noall +answer     # api.example.com. 247 IN A 203.0.113.7

# Compare against the origin: the authoritative TTL is the configured value, undecremented.
dig @ns1.example.com api.example.com +noall +answer   # api.example.com. 300 IN A 203.0.113.7

# The negative-cache TTL nobody checks — it comes from the SOA, not from the record.
dig example.com SOA +noall +answer
# example.com. 3600 IN SOA ns1.example.com. hostmaster.example.com. 2026090301 7200 3600 1209600 3600
#                                                                                            ^^^^ MINIMUM

# Flush the layers you actually control.
resolvectl flush-caches                          # systemd-resolved
sudo dscacheutil -flushcache                     # macOS

# The JVM setting that has caused more "DNS change didn't take" tickets than any other.
# -1 means cache forever; set an explicit value and match it to your shortest TTL.
networkaddress.cache.ttl=30
networkaddress.cache.negative.ttl=5

9. Concrete Trace (Step-by-Step with Real Data)

A cutover from 203.0.113.7 to 198.51.100.4 on a record published with a 300-second TTL, in a fleet running the JVM defaults above and a connection pool with 10-minute keepalives.

📥 [0] operator updates the A record at the authoritative server        t = 0
    │
    ▼
🔍 [1] resolver A last fetched 280 s ago → serves the OLD address for 20 s
        resolver B last fetched 5 s ago  → serves the OLD address for 295 s
        mean stale window ≈ 150 s, worst case 300 s                     t = 0–300 s
    │
    ▼
💻 [2] OS stub caches on top of that — up to the remaining TTL again    +0–300 s
    │
    ▼
☕ [3] JVM holds its own copy for networkaddress.cache.ttl (30 s here;
        would be forever at the historic default of -1)                  +30 s
    │
    ▼
🔗 [4] pooled connections already open to 203.0.113.7 keep serving
        until idle timeout or max-age closes them                        +up to 600 s
    │
    ▼
🎯 [5] last request to the old address observed at ~14 minutes
        — against a "5-minute TTL" everyone quoted in the plan

  1. The resolver layer is a distribution, not a deadline. Each resolver's remaining TTL is wherever it happens to be in its cycle, so the fleet drains gradually across the full TTL. Planning against the mean is how a cutover window gets set too short.

  2. The OS stub can double the wait, because it caches the already-decremented answer it received — the layers compose rather than overlap. Whether it caches at all depends on the base image, which is why staging and production disagree.

  3. The runtime cache turns minutes into forever. With networkaddress.cache.ttl=-1 the process never re-resolves and only a restart fixes it; the symptom is that some instances follow the change and others never do.

  4. The connection pool is bound by no TTL at all. It holds a socket to an address decided at open time, so the change reaches it only when the connection closes. That term dominates the tail and is invisible to every DNS diagnostic — which is why fourteen minutes against a "five-minute TTL" is the normal outcome, not a pathology.

10. When TO Use This

When planning any cutover. Lower the TTL, wait out the old TTL so every cached copy has expired, then make the change. Doing it in the other order gates the migration on exactly the value you were trying to shorten.

When choosing a failover mechanism, because this sum is the honest RTO. If it is larger than the requirement, the answer is anycast or a global load balancer rather than a shorter TTL.

When a change appears not to have taken effect. Compare the authoritative answer against a resolver's answer, then check the runtime and the pool — in that order. The layer that disagrees is the answer.

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

Do not use a very short TTL as a general safety measure. Below about 30 seconds the propagation benefit flattens — resolvers may floor low values and the layers above still cache — while authoritative query volume and resolver-quota consumption rise linearly. A 5-second TTL on a busy record buys almost nothing and costs measurably.

Do not rely on DNS TTLs for a seconds-level RTO. The cache sum has a long tail set by client behaviour you do not control; anycast and an L7 global load balancer both bypass caching entirely. (→ 33-dns-load-balancing.md)

Do not set a TTL without checking the SOA minimum, since the negative-cache TTL comes from there — an hour-long minimum turns any brief mistake into an hour-long outage no matter how short your record TTLs are. And do not assume an alias-style record gives you TTL control: Route 53 alias records follow the target's TTL and cannot be set independently.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "I lowered the TTL, so the change will propagate in 60 seconds."

✅ Reality: The new TTL applies only to answers handed out after the change. Every copy already cached expires on the old TTL. Lowering it helps the migration you do next week, not the one you are doing now.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): "Flushing the local DNS cache proves whether a change has propagated."

✅ Reality: It proves it for one machine's stub cache and nothing else. The recursive resolver's copy, the runtime's copy and the connection pool are all untouched — and the pool is not a DNS cache at all, so no flush of any kind reaches it. Testing from a freshly flushed laptop is the classic way to declare a migration complete while production is still on the old address.

❌ Misconception: "Negative caching uses the missing record's TTL."

✅ Reality: There is no record to take a TTL from. RFC 2308 derives it from the zone's SOA — min(SOA MINIMUM, the SOA's own TTL) — which is a value most people have never looked at and which is commonly an hour or more.

13. Tech Discussion Traps

Quoting the TTL as the propagation time. It is one term of four and the only one you control. Stopping there means you have not thought about the runtime or the connection pool, which is where the long tail lives.

Forgetting negative caching. It turns a two-minute mistake into an hour-long incident, it runs on a TTL taken from a different record, and it almost never comes up unless you raise it — so raising it is a strong signal.

Recommending a very short TTL as the default. It reads as caution and is a cost with diminishing returns: resolvers may floor it, the upper layers still cache, and query volume rises against a quota. The senior version chooses per record, by how urgently it might need to change.

Describing "DNS propagation" as something that spreads outward. Nothing is pushed anywhere — caches expire independently and re-query on their own schedule, which is why a fleet drains gradually and why propagation cannot be forced. The connection pool is the same blind spot one layer up: the largest term in most real cutovers, and the one no DNS tool can see.

14. Key Numbers & Benchmarks

Metric Value Context Source
Maximum TTL 2,147,483,647 s (2³¹−1) Top bit set should be treated as 0, not as a huge value RFC 2181 §8
Negative-cache TTL min(SOA MINIMUM, SOA record TTL) Derived from the SOA, never from the missing record RFC 2308 §5
Sensible negative TTL 1–3 hours; over 1 day is problematic The RFC's own operational guidance RFC 2308 §6
TTL 0 Legal — means do not cache Correct occasionally, expensive at scale RFC 1034 §4.3.4
Mean stale window Half the record TTL; worst case the full TTL Resolvers expire independently, not together Cache arithmetic
AWS resolver query quota 1,024 pps per network interface Why short TTLs are not free inside a VPC AWS VPC DNS docs
Route 53 alias TTL Not settable — uses the target's Usually desirable, occasionally a surprise Route 53 alias docs

15. Trade-offs & Performance Considerations

Dimension Trade-off
⏱️ Latency Long TTLs mean near-total cache hits and near-zero DNS latency; short TTLs put a full lookup back on the connection path
💰 Cost Query volume scales inversely with TTL, and it is billed per query at most authoritative providers — plus it consumes a fixed resolver quota inside a VPC
🔒 Security / visibility A long TTL extends the blast radius of a poisoned or hijacked answer; a short one limits it. Rarely the deciding factor, but real
📈 Scale Cache hit rate is what makes DNS scale at all. Halving the TTL roughly doubles authoritative query load for no propagation benefit past a point
🔧 Ops complexity The pre-migration TTL reduction is a two-step process with a mandatory wait; skipping it is the most common migration planning error
🐛 Debuggability Resolver caches are inspectable (dig, decrementing TTLs); runtime caches and connection pools are not, which is exactly where the tail lives

16. Real World Usage

Every planned migration runs this playbook, written down or not. Lower the TTL, wait out the previous TTL in full, cut over, confirm residual traffic has drained, restore the TTL. Teams that skip the wait find the migration window governed by the old value — usually the one they were unhappy with.

The JVM is the best-documented case of a runtime cache defeating DNS. For years the default cached successful lookups for the process lifetime, so long-running Java services kept resolving to decommissioned addresses through every flush and every TTL expiry. Modern JDKs default to a finite value, but networkaddress.cache.ttl is still the first thing to check when some instances follow a change and others do not. Negative caching produces the mirror-image incident: a record wrong for a few minutes is held as NXDOMAIN for the SOA minimum — commonly an hour — so recovery is partial and geographically random while the origin reads green.

17. Acronym Decoder

SOA — Start of Authority. Authority is the operative word: the record marks where a zone's authoritative data begins, and it carries the zone-wide parameters rather than any host's address — serial, refresh, retry, expire, and the MINIMUM field that this note cares about. Knowing the expansion is what makes it obvious why the negative-cache TTL lives there: negative answers are a property of the zone, not of a record that does not exist.

TTL — Time To Live. Worth one line only to correct the intuition: it is a maximum hold granted to caches, not a countdown to a push. Nothing expires centrally and nothing is propagated; each cache independently decides to ask again.

18. Connections (Typed Knowledge Graph)

  • What DNS resolution actually does (30-dns-resolution.md) — the walk that caching exists to avoid.

  • Record types you'll use (31-record-types.md) — particularly SOA, whose MINIMUM field sets the negative TTL.

⬇️ Builds toward (read these next to deepen this concept)

  • DNS-based load balancing & failover (33-dns-load-balancing.md) — client caching is precisely the weakness that makes DNS a slow failover mechanism.

  • DNS as an outage cause (35-dns-as-an-outage-cause.md) — the negative-caching pattern is one of the catalogued failures.

  • Connection pooling & keep-alive (Section 14) — the cache that no TTL bounds.

🔀 Alternatives / Competing approaches

  • Anycast (02-ip-packets-routing/breadth.md) — moves traffic in routing-convergence time with no cache to wait out.

  • A stable address behind an L7 global load balancer (Section 11) — failover per request rather than per TTL.

  • Service discovery with push semantics (a control plane, a mesh) — replaces expiry with invalidation for internal names.

🧩 Composes with (used together in real systems)

  • HTTP caching (Section 7) — same expiry-versus-invalidation problem one layer up, with the same lesson about layered caches.

  • Health checks (Section 11) — the detection term that sits in front of the propagation sum.

  • Where latency actually goes (Section 14) — cache hit rate is why DNS is usually free and occasionally expensive.

19. System Design Application

How this concept appears in a system design tech discussion

The framing is "how do you fail over between regions", and TTL arithmetic separates a defensible answer from a hopeful one. A strong answer states the propagation sum, gives an RTO in minutes with a tail, names the connection pool as the dominant term, and says when it would reach for anycast instead. A weak answer says "we set a 60-second TTL" and calls that the recovery time.

Topology diagram

The four amber and red nodes are the design's real subject: each holds an independent copy, they compose rather than overlap, and only the first one is bounded by the TTL you configured. The connection pool is red because nothing in DNS reaches it.

Capacity / cost back-of-envelope

Scale Constraint Solution
10x clients Authoritative query volume, billed per query and scaling inversely with TTL Raise TTLs on records that never change; keep short TTLs only on failover records
100x, containerised The resolver quota — 1,024 pps per network interface on AWS, shared with IMDS and NTP; dense nodes share one budget Node-local DNS cache in front of the cluster resolver; connection pooling so lookups happen per pool, not per request
1000x, global Propagation tail dominates every cutover, and residual traffic to a drained region becomes a correctness problem, not just a cost Move failover off DNS: anycast or a global L7 load balancer with a stable address, keeping DNS for stable naming only

Where this typically breaks at scale

  • A cutover that "completed" but did not, at 10x. Residual traffic to the old address continues for many minutes past the TTL, driven by runtime caches and open pooled connections.

  • Resolver quota exhaustion at 100x. Short TTLs plus per-request resolution plus container density exceeds a fixed per-interface budget; queries are dropped silently and appear as p99 latency shelves at the stub retry interval.

  • The 3am version: negative caching. A record is wrong for two minutes; resolvers that asked during the window hold NXDOMAIN for the SOA minimum, and recovery is partial and random for an hour after the fix.

Monitoring & SLOs

  • Residual traffic to the old target after a cutover — the only real measurement of the propagation sum, and what turns a theoretical RTO into a measured one.

  • DNS query rate per node against the resolver quota — alarm below the ceiling, since exceeding it drops queries rather than erroring.

  • Authoritative query volume per record — the direct cost of your TTL choices, and the early signal that a short TTL spread further than intended.

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • The routing policies, as a menu — Amazon Route 53: Choosing a routing policy

  • Why the apex needs a special record — Amazon Route 53: Choosing between alias and non-alias records

  • Caching is the constraint — RFC 1034 §4.3.4: Domain Names — Concepts and Facilities

  • The alternative that does not wait for caches — Cloudflare: What is Anycast?

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
The structural weakness of DNS load balancing? Client caching — you cannot recall an answer already handed out.
What does the resolver's location tell you? Where the resolver is, not where the user is.
Route 53 multivalue answer returns how many records? Up to eight healthy records, chosen at random.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

DNS load balancing distributes traffic by returning different answers to different queries — round robin across multiple A records, weighted for a canary, or latency and geolocation routing to send a client to a nearby region, usually with health checks removing unhealthy targets. It is cheap, needs no new infrastructure, and works for any protocol because it operates before the connection exists. Its weakness is structural: once an answer is cached you cannot take it back, so the granularity is per resolver rather than per request and failover takes as long as the caching chain.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification

Why is DNS a poor load balancer even though it distributes traffic?

Because the unit of distribution is a resolver, not a request. One large ISP resolver may serve a million users from a single cached answer, so a round-robin set of three A records does not produce a one-third split — it produces whatever split the resolver population happens to impose, which can be badly skewed and is not something you can observe from your side. Weighted routing has the same problem: the weights govern which answer a query gets, and queries do not arrive in proportion to users.

There is also no feedback. A real load balancer sees connection counts, response times and errors, and can shift the next request accordingly. DNS answers a question and never learns what happened, so the best it can do is remove a target after a health check fails — and even that only affects clients whose cached answer has expired. The practical consequence is that DNS is good at coarse placement, such as which region a client should reach, and bad at balancing load between servers inside one.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

When would you use DNS-based failover, and when would you reach for anycast or a global load balancer instead?

📍 Seen in the wild: the standard follow-up once someone proposes "DNS failover" against a stated RTO.

DNS failover is right when the requirement is measured in minutes, the targets are in different regions or providers, and you do not want to build anything new. It is the only mechanism that works across providers — you can fail from AWS to a different cloud with a record change, which no single load balancer can do — and with health checks at the authoritative provider it needs no human in the loop. Set the failover records to a short TTL, attach health checks, and accept an RTO of minutes with a tail.

It is the wrong tool when the requirement is seconds, because the recovery time is the sum of health-check detection, the remaining record TTL, the OS and runtime caches, and open pooled connections that no TTL bounds at all. Anycast moves traffic in routing-convergence time by withdrawing an announcement, with no cache anywhere to wait out; a global L7 load balancer keeps one stable address and re-routes per request. Both cost more infrastructure and neither works across unrelated providers. So the rule I use is: DNS for coarse geographic placement and cross-provider escape, anycast or an L7 global balancer for anything with a tight RTO. (→ 32-ttl-and-caching-layers.md)

4. Quick Comparison Table

Policy Distributes by Feedback? When you'd actually pick it
Simple One answer, always No A single target; the default
Weighted Configured proportions per query No Canary and blue/green shifts, coarse-grained
Latency Measured latency from the resolver's region Indirect Multi-region services where nearest-region is the goal
Geolocation The resolver's inferred location No Data residency and content-by-country, not performance
Geoproximity Resource location, with a bias knob No Shifting traffic between regions gradually
IP-based The client's own address range No Geolocation where resolver location misleads
Failover Health-check state, active/passive Yes, via health checks Disaster recovery to a standby
Multivalue answer Up to eight healthy records, random Yes, via health checks Cheap health-aware spreading, not real balancing

6. Mechanism & Math (How It Actually Works)

The arithmetic that matters is that traffic splits by resolver population, not by weight. If a resolver serving 40% of your users caches one answer, that answer gets 40% of the traffic for its TTL regardless of the weights you configured. The configured proportions apply to queries, and query volume is roughly proportional to the number of distinct resolvers times the query rate each generates — a quantity you neither control nor observe. Weighted DNS therefore produces the intended ratio only in aggregate over long periods and with many resolvers, which is why it is acceptable for a slow canary and useless for anything needing accuracy.

Geolocation and latency routing key on the resolver, not the user, which is the second structural gap. A user in Mumbai configured to use a resolver in Virginia is placed as if they were in Virginia. EDNS Client Subnet exists to pass a truncated client prefix to the authoritative server and largely fixes this, but it is not universally supported and some public resolvers deliberately do not send it for privacy reasons. IP-based routing policies exist precisely because resolver location is an unreliable proxy.

Failover time is a sum, not a TTL. Detection at the health checker, plus the remaining record TTL, plus every cache below it — which is why the honest RTO for DNS failover is minutes with a long tail, and why the number worth measuring is residual traffic to the failed target rather than the moment the record changed.

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

Do not use DNS to balance load between servers behind one address. There is no feedback loop, the granularity is per resolver, and a single large resolver can skew the split arbitrarily. That is what an L4 or L7 load balancer is for, and it observes what DNS cannot. (→ Load balancing algorithms, Section 11)

Do not promise a seconds-level RTO with DNS failover. The recovery time includes caches you do not control and open connections no TTL touches. If the requirement is tight, the answer is anycast or a global load balancer, and saying so is stronger than tuning a TTL downward.

Do not use geolocation routing for latency. It routes on the resolver's inferred location and answers a residency question, not a performance one. Latency routing measures actual paths; use that when the goal is speed, and reserve geolocation for legal and content requirements.

Do not run health-checked DNS without watching the failed target. A health check tells you the record changed. Residual traffic tells you whether clients acted on it, and only the second one is the recovery.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "Round-robin DNS distributes traffic evenly across the servers."

✅ Reality: It distributes answers evenly across queries, and one cached answer at a large resolver serves an arbitrary number of users. Real splits are skewed, unobservable from your side, and drift with the resolver population rather than with your configuration.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): "Latency-based routing measures the user's latency."

✅ Reality: It measures from the resolver, because the resolver is the only party the authoritative server sees. A user on a distant public resolver gets placed by that resolver's location. EDNS Client Subnet narrows the gap where it is supported, which is why IP-based routing policies exist as an alternative.

18. Connections (Typed Knowledge Graph)

⬇️ Builds toward (read these next to deepen this concept)

  • Anycast (02-ip-packets-routing/breadth.md) — traffic steering with no cache to wait out.

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • Cluster DNS names and search domains — Kubernetes: DNS for Services and Pods

  • The resolver that serves them — CoreDNS manual

  • .local is reserved for multicast DNS — RFC 6762: Multicast DNS

  • The standards-based discovery pattern — RFC 6763: DNS-Based Service Discovery

  • The resolver and its hard quota — Amazon VPC: Amazon DNS concepts

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
A Kubernetes Service's FQDN? <service>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local
Why is .local a bad choice for a private zone? RFC 6762 reserves it for link-local multicast DNS.
What is split-horizon DNS? The same name resolving differently inside and outside the network.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

Private DNS is a zone that only resolves inside your network, served by a resolver that also forwards public names outward — so db.internal answers inside the VPC and NXDOMAIN everywhere else. Kubernetes builds service discovery directly on it: every Service gets a name at <service>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local, resolved by CoreDNS, with search domains configured so short names work within a namespace. The thing that bites is that the same short name resolves differently depending on where you run it, and that per-request lookups against a resolver with a fixed query quota is a real production limit.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification

How does a pod resolve payments into an address, and what happens on the wire?

The pod's /etc/resolv.conf points at the cluster DNS service and carries a search list — <namespace>.svc.cluster.local, svc.cluster.local, cluster.local — plus an ndots option that decides when a name is treated as already-qualified. A short name like payments has no dots, so the stub resolver appends each search domain in turn: it tries payments.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local first, which CoreDNS answers from the cluster's Service records, and resolution stops there.

The cost shows up for external names. api.stripe.com has fewer dots than the ndots threshold that Kubernetes configures, so the stub tries it against every search domain first — producing several NXDOMAIN round trips before the correct query is sent. That is why a fully-qualified name with a trailing dot, or raising the pod's dnsConfig options, is a standard fix for external-call latency in clusters. Read the actual ndots value out of a running pod's resolv.conf rather than quoting one, because it varies with cluster configuration and the number is what determines how many wasted lookups you are paying for.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

DNS-based service discovery versus a service registry or mesh — what decides it?

🎯 Really testing: whether you can name what DNS cannot express, rather than treating discovery as a naming problem only.

DNS wins on universality. Every language, every runtime and every legacy binary can resolve a hostname with no library, no sidecar and no SDK, which is why Kubernetes chose it and why it remains the lowest-friction option for anything polyglot. It is also stateless from the client's point of view: no registration, no heartbeat, no watch.

What it cannot express is health and load in real time. A DNS answer is a snapshot governed by TTLs, so a backend that just died is still in the answer until the record and every cache expire, and there is no way to convey "this instance is at 90% capacity". Registries and meshes solve exactly that: they push changes rather than waiting for expiry, and they carry per-endpoint state that routing can act on. So the split I use is DNS for stable service names and coarse discovery, a mesh or registry when you need fast endpoint churn, per-request load awareness, or traffic policy — and I would not add a mesh purely for discovery, because that is the part DNS already does well. (→ Service mesh, Section 11)

4. Quick Comparison Table

Mechanism Change propagation Carries health/load? Client requirement When you'd actually pick it
Private DNS zone TTL expiry No Nothing — any runtime Stable internal names across mixed technology
Kubernetes cluster DNS Seconds, via CoreDNS watching the API Only via readiness gating Endpoints Nothing The default inside a cluster
Headless Service + SRV Same, but exposes per-pod records Same A client that reads SRV Stateful sets, per-pod addressing
Service registry (Consul, etcd) Push, sub-second Yes A client library or sidecar Fast churn, health-aware routing
Service mesh Push, sub-second Yes, plus policy A sidecar or ambient dataplane When you need traffic policy, not just names
mDNS / .local Multicast, link-local only No mDNS support Devices on one link — never a datacentre

6. Mechanism & Math (How It Actually Works)

The multiplier is the thing to carry. Each search-domain attempt is a separate query, so one logical lookup of an external name can cost several round trips plus the successful one, and every one of them counts against the cluster resolver and — once forwarded — against the VPC resolver's quota. AWS documents that quota as 1,024 packets per second per network interface, shared with the metadata and time services and not increasable. Multiply a few wasted lookups by pod density by per-request resolution and a node reaches it without the application doing anything unusual.

Split-horizon is the second structural idea. The same name can resolve to a private address inside and either a public address or nothing outside, because two different resolvers are consulted. It is what makes private endpoints work, and it is also why "it resolves on my laptop but not in the cluster" and its reverse are both routine — the name is fine, the resolver is different.

Naming choice matters more than it looks. RFC 6762 reserves .local for link-local multicast DNS and requires those queries to go to a multicast address rather than to a resolver, so a private zone named .local collides with mDNS behaviour on any host that implements it. Kubernetes' cluster.local is a subdomain of that reserved space and works because clusters configure their resolvers explicitly, but a new private zone should use a name you actually control — a subdomain of a domain you own — rather than .local or an invented TLD.

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

Do not resolve on every request. DNS caching plus connection pooling is the difference between one lookup per pool and one per call, and the quota is fixed. A node-local DNS cache is the standard remedy and it is cheap; raising the quota is not an option.

Do not name a private zone .local or an invented TLD. .local is reserved for mDNS and behaves differently on hosts that implement it, and an invented TLD stops working the day ICANN delegates it. Use a subdomain of a domain you own.

Do not rely on DNS alone for fast endpoint churn. Records change at TTL granularity and carry no health signal, so a rapidly scaling or crash-looping workload will hand out addresses that are already gone. That is the case for readiness gating plus a registry or mesh, not for a shorter TTL.

Do not put internal names in a public zone. It leaks topology and it invites the split-horizon confusion where a name resolves publicly to something stale. Keep the private zone private and let external names be the only thing that leaves.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "A short service name is one DNS lookup."

✅ Reality: The search list means a short name is tried against each suffix in turn. In-cluster names usually hit on the first attempt; external names are the expensive case, because they are tried against every search domain before being sent as given. That multiplier, not the resolver's speed, is what makes DNS show up in a cluster's latency profile.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): "Kubernetes service discovery is a special mechanism."

✅ Reality: It is ordinary DNS with a zone that CoreDNS generates from the API server's Services and Endpoints. Once you see it as a private zone with a watcher keeping it current, the failure modes stop being mysterious — they are caching, search domains, resolver capacity, and readiness gating.

18. Connections (Typed Knowledge Graph)

  • Record types you'll use (31-record-types.md) — SRV and PTR are the discovery-shaped types.

⬇️ Builds toward (read these next to deepen this concept)

  • CoreDNS & in-cluster service discovery and Headless services & StatefulSet DNS (Section 13) — the same material with the cluster's implementation detail.

  • Private DNS in the cloud and PrivateLink / VPC endpoints (Section 12) — split-horizon resolution as a cloud networking primitive.

  • Service mesh (Section 11) — what you add when TTL-granularity discovery is not enough.
