📋 TABLE / PLAYBOOK override applied. This topic's honest answer is a catalogue you can recall under pressure, so Section 4 is promoted to the centrepiece and moved above Section 3, and Section 6 is reduced to a triage flowchart. Per the override rule the table does not count against the word budget.

📚 Reference Links

  • Delegation failing from above — Cloudflare: Understanding how Facebook disappeared from the Internet

  • The same failure on the resolver side — Cloudflare: 1.1.1.1 incident on July 14, 2025

  • When DNS errors are the symptom, not the cause — AWS: Summary of the AWS Service Event in the Northern Virginia (US-EAST-1) Region, December 2021

  • Why a two-minute mistake lasts an hour — RFC 2308: Negative Caching of DNS Queries

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
SERVFAIL vs NXDOMAIN — who is telling you what? SERVFAIL: the resolver could not get an answer. NXDOMAIN: the name authoritatively does not exist.
Why does a brief bad record outlast the fix? Negative caching, on a TTL from the SOA rather than from the record.
The failure where records were perfect? Facebook 2021 — BGP withdrew the routes to their own nameservers.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

"It's always DNS" is a joke about a real property: DNS is the first dependency of every request, it has no degraded mode, and most of its failure modes are invisible from the origin. The catalogue is short — expiry, propagation, negative caching, resolver capacity, delegation and reachability — and each has a distinct signature, so triage is mostly about matching the symptom rather than probing. The sharper version of the joke is that DNS is often the symptom: in AWS's December 2021 event, elevated internal DNS errors were the visible face of network congestion, not its cause.

4. The Catalogue — DNS Failure Patterns

This is the section to re-read the morning of. Symptom in the first column, mechanism in the second, the check that confirms it in the third.

# Symptom Mechanism Confirming check Fix / prevention
1 Everything fails at once, worldwide, records unchanged Nameservers unreachable — routes withdrawn or network partition (Facebook 2021) Resolvers return SERVFAIL; authoritative servers unreachable from outside Two independent DNS providers on the delegation
2 Domain stops resolving on a date nobody noticed Domain or certificate-adjacent expiry — registration lapsed, auto-renew card failed whois expiry date; registrar status codes Registry lock, auto-renew alerting owned by a team not a person
3 New resolutions fail, existing sessions fine Registrar or registry delegation change — NS records at the parent wrong dig +trace diverges at the TLD referral Change control on NS records; monitor the parent's NS set
4 Change deployed, some clients still on the old target Propagation — caches expiring independently across the fleet Compare authoritative answer vs resolver answer; residual traffic to the old target Lower TTL before the migration and wait out the old one
5 Fix deployed, recovery partial and geographically random for ~an hour Negative caching — NXDOMAIN cached from the SOA MINIMUM dig example.com SOA, read MINIMUM Keep SOA MINIMUM modest; treat record deletion as a deploy
6 Some instances follow a change, others never do Runtime cache — JVM networkaddress.cache.ttl or equivalent Check the runtime setting; restart one instance and compare Set an explicit finite value; never -1
7 Traffic keeps hitting a decommissioned address long after cutover Connection pool holding sockets opened to the old address Connection age and pool metrics; no DNS tool will show it Max connection age; drain rather than assume
8 Tail latency shelf at the resolver retry interval, no errors logged Resolver query quota — dropped queries silently retried Query rate per node vs the documented quota (1,024 pps per ENI on AWS) Node-local DNS cache; pool connections so lookups are per-pool
9 External calls slow in-cluster, fine elsewhere Search-domain multiplier — short names tried against every suffix resolv.conf search list and ndots; count queries per external lookup Fully-qualify external names, or tune dnsConfig
10 One domain resolves for small answers, hangs for large ones UDP/TCP fallback blocked — TC bit set, TCP filtered or fragments dropped dig +tcp for that name; compare with +ignore Permit DNS over TCP; set a sane EDNS buffer size
11 Resolves publicly, fails internally (or the reverse) Split-horizon mismatch — wrong resolver for the zone dig @<internal> vs dig @1.1.1.1 Keep private names out of the public zone; correct resolver config
12 Health checks green, users routed to a dead region Health check scope — checking the LB, not the dependency behind it What the check actually requests; compare with a real user path Deep checks, and alarm on residual traffic post-failover
13 Public resolver unavailable, your services can't resolve anything Single resolver dependency (Cloudflare 1.1.1.1, July 2025 — 62 minutes) Which resolver resolv.conf names; is there a second? Provider resolver plus node-local cache; a real secondary
14 Widespread third-party outage, your DNS is fine Authoritative provider DDoS or outage (the Dyn pattern) Whose nameservers serve your zone — and how many distinct operators Multi-provider authoritative DNS
15 "DNS errors" in dashboards during an unrelated incident DNS as symptom — congestion or overload upstream (AWS, Dec 2021) Do non-DNS paths fail too? Is the resolver itself healthy? Do not anchor on DNS; check whether the network under it is degraded

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification

Given "the site is down", how do you decide in two minutes whether DNS is involved?

Three checks in order, and each one eliminates a block of the catalogue. First, dig +trace the name: if it diverges at the root or TLD referral, the problem is delegation or nameserver reachability — patterns 1, 3 and 14 — and nothing inside your infrastructure is relevant. If the walk completes, second, compare the authoritative answer with what a public resolver returns: agreement means the data is right and you are looking at a caching or client problem (4 through 7), disagreement means the change has not reached that resolver yet.

Third, read the response code rather than treating any failure as "DNS is down". SERVFAIL means the resolver tried and could not get an answer, which points at reachability or DNSSEC validation; NXDOMAIN means someone authoritatively said the name does not exist, which is a data or negative-caching problem; a correct answer with a failing connection means DNS is fine and you should be looking at the network or the service. That third case is the most common outcome, and it is the reason the discipline is worth having — it stops an incident anchoring on DNS for twenty minutes.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

Which of these do you actually engineer against, given you cannot prevent all fifteen?

🎯 Really testing: whether you can rank by blast radius rather than listing mitigations.

I rank by whether the failure is total and whether recovery is in your hands. Patterns 1, 2, 3 and 14 — unreachable nameservers, expiry, delegation, provider outage — are total, external, and slow to recover, so they get real investment: two independent DNS providers on the delegation, registry lock with renewal alerting owned by a team, and change control on NS records. That is a small amount of setup against the failures that produce a complete outage you cannot fix by deploying.

The caching family (4 through 7) is not preventable and does not need to be; it needs to be planned for, which costs nothing but discipline — lower TTLs before migrations, keep the SOA minimum modest, set explicit runtime cache values, cap connection age. Capacity failures (8, 9) get a node-local DNS cache, which is a small standing cost against a limit you cannot raise. What I would not do is chase patterns 10 through 12 preventively; they are configuration mistakes best caught by the triage table when they happen, and building infrastructure against them is a poor use of the same hours.

6. Mechanism & Math (How It Actually Works)

Reduced to the triage flowchart per the TABLE/PLAYBOOK override — the mechanisms themselves live in the notes this one aggregates, and repeating them here would duplicate 30-dns-resolution.md and 32-ttl-and-caching-layers.md.

The branch that earns its place is the last one. "Correct answer" is the most common outcome and the point at which most incidents should leave DNS behind — but two residual patterns hide there, and both present without DNS errors: a tail-latency shelf from resolver quota or search-domain multiplication, and traffic still arriving at an old target because a runtime cache or a connection pool never re-resolved.

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

Do not anchor an incident on DNS because a dashboard says "DNS errors". AWS's December 2021 event is the counter-example worth carrying: elevated internal DNS errors were the visible symptom of network congestion overwhelming devices, and the team's own summary makes the distinction. Ask whether non-DNS paths are also failing before committing the incident to a DNS theory.

Do not treat this catalogue as a prevention checklist. Engineering against all fifteen is a poor allocation; patterns 1, 2, 3 and 14 are worth real investment because they are total and externally caused, the caching family needs discipline rather than infrastructure, and the rest are triage material.

Do not test propagation from a freshly flushed laptop. It proves one stub cache is empty and nothing about resolvers, runtimes or connection pools — which is how migrations get declared complete while production is still on the old address. (→ 32-ttl-and-caching-layers.md)

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "It's always DNS."

✅ Reality: DNS is disproportionately visible during incidents because it is the first thing in every request path and it fails totally rather than partially. It is also frequently the symptom of something underneath it, as in AWS's December 2021 event. The useful version of the saying is "check DNS first because it is cheap to rule out", not "assume DNS".

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): "If the fix is deployed and the origin is healthy, the incident is over."

✅ Reality: Negative caching, runtime caches and open connection pools all keep serving the broken state after the origin is correct, and each runs on a different clock. Recovery is partial and randomly distributed across users, which reads like a flapping service and is actually four caches draining independently.

18. Connections (Typed Knowledge Graph)

  • TTL & caching layers (32-ttl-and-caching-layers.md) — patterns 4 through 7 in mechanism form.

  • Triage playbooks (Section 15) — the same discipline applied to 502/503/504 and the other standard symptom sets.

  • Cascading failures & thundering herds (Section 14) — how a DNS failure becomes a retry storm one layer up.

  • Health checks (Section 11) — pattern 12, and why a shallow check makes failover worse than none.
